The horn is not a warning. People think it is, but a horn in fog is a question, and every ship out there is obliged to answer it.

I have kept this light for eleven years. In eleven years I have learned the answers the way you learn a language you never wanted to speak: the ferry, flat and impatient; the trawlers, quick and twice over; the navy boats, once, and late. In November the fog came in and something answered that I did not know.

It was not far off. It was close enough that the horn's own note was still moving when the answer came back, and the answer was the same note, sung rather than sounded, by something that had heard mine first and had been waiting a long time for a reason to speak.

I did not sound the horn again that night. I have not sounded it since. The light still turns, because the light is machinery and machinery does not get frightened, and every evening at the same hour something out in the water answers a question I have stopped asking.

The relief keeper arrives in March. I have written him a note. I have not decided what to put in it.
